results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You must keep business records for at least as long as they could be needed to support a tax return or to prove that you paid the tax you reported. In practice that means:

* Keep records that back up any amount reported on a tax return until the that return’s period of limitation expires (usually 3 years after filing, or 6 years if you under‑reported income, etc.) – see Table 3 for the exact periods.  
* Keep employment‑tax records (payroll, forms 941/944, etc.) for at least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid.  
* Keep asset‑related records (depreciation, basis, sale documents) until the limitation period for the year you sold or otherwise disposed of the asset ends.  
* Keep copies of every filed tax return because they help prepare future returns.  
* After the IRS no longer needs the records for tax purposes, you may destroy them only after checking that other agencies (e.g., insurance or creditors) don't have a longer‑term requirement.  

These rules give a minimum retention period; you can retain records longer if required for other legal or business reasons. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records so you can:

1. **Show what you earned and spent**   
   - Records such as receipts, invoices, and bank statements back up the amounts you report in your books and on your tax return.  
   - “It is important to keep these documents because they support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

2. **Prepare accurate tax filings**   
   - Good records let you fill out the tax forms that your business must file and help you answer the IRS if it questions any item.  
   - “You need good records to prepare your tax returns.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

3. **Make informed business decisions**   
   - By tracking sales, expenses, and profits, you can see whether your business is improving, which products sell best, or where you need to change.  
   - “Good records will help you … Monitor the progress of your business.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

4. **Generate the financial statements you need**   
   - Income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets are built from recorded transactions, and they are required by banks, creditors, or investors.  
   - “You need good records to prepare accurate financial statements.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

5. **Satisfy legal and regulatory requirements**   
   - The IRS, state tax authorities, and other regulators may ask for your records to verify your calculations or to confirm that you are following the rules.  
   - “The records must support the entries in your books and on your tax return. You must keep them … available at all times for inspection by the IRS.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

So keeping solid business records keeps your taxes compliant, lets you manage and grow your business, and meets the legal obligations that come with being an owner.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 12)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The IRS lets you choose one of several accounting methods when you file your first Schedule C (Form 1040).  For most small businesses the choice is between

- **Cash method** – record income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them.  It’s simple and works well if you don’t keep inventory.  
- **Accrual method** – record income in the year you earn it and expenses in the year you incur them, even if payment comes later.  You’re required to use accrual if your business must keep inventory, unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer.  
- **Combination or special methods** – you may mix cash and accrual for different items or use special treatments for things like inventory, depreciation, or bad debts, as long as the method clearly shows your income and you keep consistent books.  

If you file a first tax return with a cash method and later want to switch, you’ll usually need IRS approval (Form 3115) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  If you have inventory but qualify as a small business, you can still use the cash method and treat inventory as non‑incidental material or supplies [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  Otherwise, you must use the accrual method for sales and purchases of inventory [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To identify hazards in your workplace you can follow a simple, step‑by‑step process that is built into OSHA’s small‑business guidance:

1. **Start with a routine self‑inspection.**  
   Use the handbook’s workplace self‑inspection checklists to walk through each area of your business. They help you spot hazards and decide which controls to put in place. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Make inspections part of your safety program.**  
   OSHA’s recommended practices say that regular inspections are an essential tool for finding and fixing hazards before an injury occurs. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

3. **Include your workers in the process.**  
   Let employees help identify problems, report them, and suggest practical controls. Checklists and inspections should involve the people who actually work on the job. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

4. **Check specific areas that often hide hazards.**  
   • Walkways and working surfaces – keep them clear, dry and free of dropped items.  
   • Roadways, stairs, and access routes – maintain adequate lighting, guardrails, and head‑room.  
   • Spills, stored materials, and ventilation – clean immediately, store properly, and keep airflow to limit dust or fumes.  
   These details are in the handbook’s “Walkways” sections. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)

5. **Use additional resources if needed.**  
   If you want more help, OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program can walk through your workplace with you and suggest improvements at no cost. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

**Bottom line:**  
Perform a quick, structured self‑inspection each week, use the checklists, involve your workers, and review the results to keep your workplace safe. This routine practice is the best way to find hazards early and prevent accidents.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash accounting and accrual accounting are the two main ways a business tracks its income and expenses for tax purposes.

**Cash method**  
- You record income the year you actually receive it (or it’s constructively available).  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses the year you pay them.  
- The method is simple because it follows the movement of cash.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

**Accrual method**  
- You record income in the year you earn it, even if payment comes later.  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them, whether or not you have paid them yet.  
- This method matches income to the expenses that produced it, giving a clearer picture of profitability.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

So, with **cash accounting** the timing of money coming in or going out dictates the tax year, while with **accrual accounting** the timing of earning earnings and incurring costs decides the tax year.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes, you can deduct the ordinary and necessary expenses that are part of a business trip. This includes transportation (airplane, train, bus, car, taxi, etc.), lodging, meals (typically 50 % of the cost unless you use the standard meal allowance), as well as related items such as baggage fees, business‑related parking, tolls, and tips. The deduction is limited to the business‑use portion of any expenses that are also used personally. You can find the details in the IRS guidance: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) and a brief summary in [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).



**Sources:**

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary is a short, one‑to‑two‑paragraph overview that tells the reader the key points of the business plan. It should cover:

* The core business idea  
* How much money you need and how you will use it  
* How much money you have already invested or will invest  
* A brief schedule of your goals  

This section is usually written last to reflect information that becomes clear after the rest of the plan is finished. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
You can describe your target market by following these steps:

1. Identify the niche or group that is the best fit for your product or service.  
2. List the key characteristics of that group, such as age, gender, income, lifestyle, or industry.  
3. Estimate how many people or businesses fit those criteria and how fast that group is growing so you know how much market share you could realistically capture.  

These points come from the “Target Market” section, which explains how to define the niche, describe customer characteristics, and estimate the market size and growth potential. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes. Your shop is a private business that serves the public, so it is a **public accommodation** under the ADA. The ADA requires that all such businesses remove “readily achievable” barriers to access, which normally means making at least one entrance wheelchair‑accessible and providing an accessible route inside the shop. If a door or entrance is not accessible, you must provide an alternative accessible entrance or a suitable alternative service [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).



**Sources:**
1. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)
2. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 10)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

results.answer:
The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires businesses to follow its employment‑related rules once the business has **15 or more employees**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19)

results.answer:
All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA within **8 hours** of the incident. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You are exempt from OSHA injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping only if you meet one of the two conditions below:

* You had **10 or fewer employees for the entire last calendar year** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).  
* Your business is in a **low‑hazard industry** listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

Even if you qualify for that exemption, you must still report **fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** to OSHA within the required time frames [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.answer:
Injury and illness records must be kept at the worksite for **at least five years**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**Tax records** – Keep:
- Copies of all filed tax returns and any supporting documents that explain income, expenses, and deductions.  
- Employment‑tax records (e.g., payroll, W‑2s, Forms 941/944) for at least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid.  
- Asset records (purchase, improvement, depreciation, sale details) until the period of limitations expires for the year in which the property is disposed of.  
- Any other records needed to administer a provision of the Internal Revenue Code.  
These must be kept as long as they may be needed to support a tax return or to respond to an IRS inquiry [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

**Injury‑related OSHA records** – Keep:
- OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses), Form 301 (Incident Report), and Form 300A (Summary) for each calendar year.  
- Supervisor’s reports, medical records, injury investigations, and safety‑training records.  
These records must be retained at the workplace for **at least five (5) years** after the year they cover (or longer if required by specific regulations) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

**Summary of retention periods**

| Record type | Minimum retention period |
|-------------|--------------------------|
| Tax returns & supporting documents | As long as needed for tax administration (usually 3–7 years, depending on the limitation period) |
| Employment‑tax records | 4 years after tax due/payed |
| Asset/depreciation records | Until the asset’s disposition year’s limitation period ends |
| OSHA Form 300, 301, 300A & related injury/illness docs | 5 years after the covered calendar year |

(If employer has fewer than 10 workers or is in a low‑hazard industry, some OSHA record‑keeping requirements may be relaxed, but the five‑year minimum applies when required.)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)
3. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

1. **Pick a business structure** – decide whether you’ll be a sole proprietor, partnership, S‑corporation, C‑corporation, or LLC. Your structure determines the IRS forms you’ll file. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3)

2. **Get an Employer Identification Number (EIN)** – the EIN is your business tax ID. It’s required for most businesses, even if you have no employees. Apply online at IRS.gov/EIN. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

3. **Choose your tax year** – most new businesses adopt a calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31). Some can use a fiscal year; if you change it later, file Form 1128 to get approval. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

4. **Pick an accounting method** – cash accounting (report income when received, expenses when paid) is common for small businesses without inventory; accrual accounting records income when earned and expenses when incurred. Pick one when you file your first return and keep it consistently. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

5. **Open a separate business checking account & use a business checkbook** – keep personal and business funds separate, and record every deposit and withdrawal in the checkbook. Reconcile the account monthly. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

6. **Track all supporting documents** – keep receipts, invoices, bank statements, canceled checks, and any other paperwork that shows the amount, date, and purpose of every transaction. Use a system that lets you organize by year and type of income or expense. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

7. **Maintain a simple bookkeeping system** – at minimum, keep a daily summary of cash receipts, a monthly summary, a check‑disbursements journal, and a ledger of all accounts. You can keep separate books if you run more than one business. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=21)

8. **Store records en‑marge** – paper and electronic versions both qualify; your electronic system must keep the records legible, searchable, and reproducible, and should be tested by the IRS if needed. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=1)

9. **File the right tax returns** –  
   * Sole proprietor: Form 1040 with Schedule C and Schedule SE.  
   * Partnership: Form 1065 and K‑1s to partners.  
   * S‑corp: Form 1120‑S and K‑1s.  
   * C‑corp: Form 1120.  
   Check the due dates for each and file on time. [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)

10. **Make estimated tax payments if required** – if you expect to owe $1 000 + for a sole proprietor or $500 + for a corporation, use Form 1040‑ES (or 1120‑W for corporations) to pay quarterly. [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9)

11. **Pay employment taxes if you hire workers** – run payroll, withhold Social Security, Medicare, and federal income tax, file Forms 941 or 944, and issue W‑2s at year‑end. [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)

12. **Keep the records the required time** – generally 3–7 years, depending on the item and the liability. results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep your employees safe **and** make your premises accessible you need to follow a few key steps that are covered in the handbook:

### 1.  Create a Safety & Health Program  
- Develop a program that identifies hazards, trains workers, and monitors results.  
- Make it part of everyday operations – not a one‑time checklist.  
- Include worker participation and regular inspections.  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)

### 2.  Keep the Work Area Free of Hazards  
- Keep walkways clear, repair holes, and use non‑slip mats on wet surfaces.  
- Provide guardrails where walkways rise more than 4 ft.  
- Store materials so they don’t block aisles.  
> [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)

### 3.  Make the Facility Accessible (ADA)  
#### a.  Entrances  
- Ensure at least one entrance is accessible: a ramp (≤1:12 slope), handrails, and a wide landing.  
- If a door is stuck or locked for security, install a buzzer or call box that is reachable (≤48 in. above the floor).  
- Provide clear signage pointing to the accessible entrance.  
> [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

#### b.  Door Hardware & Turnstiles  
- Replace door knobs that require tight grasping with lever handles or loop handles.  
- Where a turnstile blocks access, install an accessible gate or replace the turnstile.  
> [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)

#### c.  Parking  
- Supply the required number of accessible parking spaces: at least one per 25 spaces, one of the eight spaces must be van‑accessible.  
- Spaces must be 8 ft. wide (car) or 5 ft. wide (van), with an 8‑ft. wide (van) aisle.  
- The path from parking to entrance must be slip‑resistant, < 1:50 slope, and free of steps.  
> [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)

#### d.  Interior Aisles & Sales Areas  
- Keep aisles at least 36 in. wide, 3‑ft turning space at corners.  
- Lower sales counters to a maximum of 36 in. above the floor and provide 30 × 48 in. clearance in front.  
> [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

#### e.  Signage & Communication  
- Use the international accessibility symbol on all accessible parking and entrances.  
- Provide written communication options (pen and paper, TDD) for customers who need it.  
> [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18)

### 4.  Use Available Resources  
- OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program (free, confidential) can help you spot hazards and plan improvements.  
- State or local accessibility codes should be followed in addition to the ADA.  
> [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

---

**Bottom line:**  
- **Safety**: set up a proactive safety program, keep walk‑routes free of hazards, and train employees.  
- **Accessibility**: modify entrances, doors, parking, aisles, and counters so a wheelchair or person with a disability can enter, move, and use your services just like everyone else.  

If you need help, reach out to OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation or a local accessibility center.

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Cover Page & Table of Contents** – Put the company name, address, phone, owners, and date on the cover. The table of contents is optional but helps navigation.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

2. **Executive Summary** – One‑two paragraphs that tell readers what the business does, how much money you need, how you’ll use it, and a quick schedule of goals. Write this last, after the rest of the plan is complete.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

3. **Business Description** – Describe the product or service, its market, competitive advantage, and any regulations that apply.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

4. **Management & Staffing** – Outline the organizational structure, key owners, managers, and their credentials.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

5. **Market Analysis** – Detail the total market, target segment, competition, and how you’ll reach customers.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

6. **Financial Section** – Include three‑year projections:  
   * **Income Statement** – shows income and expenses.  
   * **Cash‑Flow Statement** – shows when money comes in and goes out.  
   * **Balance Sheet** – shows assets, liabilities, net worth.  
   * **Break‑even Analysis** – where costs equal revenue.  
   Create a “Sources & Uses” sheet and explain assumptions in a “Notes” page.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)

7. **Exhibits** – Attach resumes, contracts, floor plans, legal documents, etc.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

**Setting Up Accounting**

1. **Open a Business Checking Account** – Keep it separate from personal funds. Use the account for all receipts, deposits, and outgoing payments.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

2. **Record Transactions Daily** – Write every expense and income entry in a business checkbook or journal. Identify the source of every deposit and type of expense.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

3. **Use Journals and Ledgers** –  
   * **Journal** – records each transaction (e.g., sales, purchases, payroll).  
   * **Ledger** – aggregates totals for each account.  
   These form the basis for your financial statements.  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

4. **Monthly Reconciliation** – Compare your bank statement with your checkbook and books to verify balances, catch errors, and record bank charges.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

5. **Choose an Accounting Method** –  
   * **Cash method** (record income when received, expenses when paid).  
   * **Accrual method** (record income when earned, expenses when incurred).  
   Pick based on whether you have inventory or not. You normally cannot change methods without IRS approval.  
   [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

6. **Maintain Supporting Documents** – Keep receipts, canceled checks, invoices, deposit slips, and any other proof of transactions. Store them by year and type.  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

7. **Prepare Periodic Financial Statements** –  
   * **Income Statement** (profit & loss).  
   * **Balance Sheet**.  
   * **Cash‑Flow Statement**.  
   These help you monitor progress, secure loans, and file taxes.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)

**Quick Checklist**

- [ ] Separate business & personal accounts  
- [ ] Record transactions daily in checkbook/journal  
- [ ] Reconcile monthly  
- [ ] Choose an appropriate accounting method (cash or accrual)  
- [ ] Keep all receipts, invoices, and supporting documents  
- [ ] Produce three‑year financial projections (income, cash flow, balance sheet)  

These steps give you a solid business plan and a reliable accounting foundation for keeping your finances in order.

results.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
results.answer:
**What to track for taxes**  
- Keep records of all ordinary and necessary business‑related taxes (state, local, personal‑property, real‑estate, excise, employment, etc.) that you can deduct on Schedule C.  
- Track the portion of car expenses that is business use (mileage, gas, tolls, parking, insurance, depreciation) so you can compute the deductible amount.  
- If you use your vehicle in the first year you must choose either the standard mileage rate or actual expenses; the rule cannot be changed in the same year for a leased vehicle.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  

**What to track for travel expenses**  
- **Transportation**: airfare, train, bus, car, taxi, limousine, and commuter‑bus fares between your home and a business destination.  
- **Baggage and shipping**: fees to send luggage, samples or display material between home and temporary work sites.  
- **Car or truck**: fuel, oil, tires, gas, insurance, maintenance, parking, tolls, and interest on a car loan (if you use the standard mileage rate you may still deduct parking, tolls, and interest).  
- **Meals and lodging**: 50 % of meal costs for overnight or long business trips; full cost of lodging if the trip requires a stay.  
- **Other person‑to‑person reimbursements**: tips, cleaning, telephone, fax, and other travel‑related costs that can be deducted.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) (details on car/truck expenses)  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) (record‑keeping rules for travel, transportation, and gift expenses)  

**General record‑keeping**  
- Keep receipts, invoices, and mileage logs for every travel or tax‑related expense.  
- Separate personal and business portions whenever an item is used for both.  

[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
Yes.  A sole‑proprietor who pays wages, files pension or excise‑tax returns, or wants a separate business identity generally must obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN).  The IRS issues EINs to sole proprietors, partnerships, corporations and LLCs, and single‑member LLCs that elect to report on a Schedule C may obtain an EIN even if they have no employees [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).  If the business hires employees or files pension or excise tax returns, an EIN is required, and the IRS also recommends obtaining one for all business filings [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

Obtaining an EIN does **not** lock you into a specific accounting method.  When you file your first income‑tax return for the business, you choose an accounting method – cash, accrual, or a permissible combination – and you must use that method consistently for income, expenses and book‑keeping.  The choice is made at the time of the first return and is independent of whether you use an EIN or a social‑security number [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
You should keep OSHA injury and illness records on the following forms and for at least five years:

- **OSHA Form 300** – raw log of all recordable injuries and illnesses.  
- **OSHA Form 301** – detailed incident report for each recordable case.  
- **OSHA Form 300A** – annual summary of injuries and illnesses.  

These records must be kept in a workplace office for a minimum of five years.  
If you also keep worker‑medical or exposure records, retain those for the period required by the specific type of record or by other applicable regulations.

results.question: how do i register a trademark
results.answer:
To register a trademark you can file with either a state agency or the federal U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).  
1. **Choose the level of protection** – decide whether you want state‑wide exclusivity (file with your state’s Secretary of State) or nationwide protection (file with the USPTO).  
2. **Search the databases** – before filing, use the trademark search tools to make sure no one else has already registered the same or a similar mark.  
3. **Submit the application** – prepare the application form, pay the filing fee, and submit it online through the appropriate agency’s portal.  
4. **Wait for examination and decision** – the agency will review the application, may request additional information, and ultimately grant or deny the registration.  

Contact information:  
- **State level (e.g., South Dakota)** – Secretary of State, 605‑773‑2797, https://sdsos.gov/ [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)  
- **Federal level** – U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, 703‑308‑HELP or 800‑786‑9199, https://www.uspto.gov [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)
